expected_evidence: Geological/geochemical impact proxies at the ~12,900 cal BP (10,950 BCE) horizon across North American sites: platinum-group element anomalies, nanodiamonds, magnetic and glassy microspherules, elevated iridium, and a 'black mat' organic-rich layer marking the Younger Dryas boundary

Marine/lacustrine sediment core evidence for an abrupt freshwater or meltwater pulse into the North Atlantic coincident with the same horizon (foraminiferal oxygen-isotope shifts, ice-rafted debris changes, reduced North Atlantic Deep Water proxies) that would mechanistically link an airburst-triggered ice-sheet disruption to AMOC slowdown
Astronomical/airburst-specific traces: shocked quartz, high-temperature meltglass, or a candidate crater/strewn field (though a true airburst may leave no crater, only ejecta/thermal signatures)

Archaeological/material evidence of disruption to Clovis-era human occupation and stratigraphic correlation of megafaunal extinction layers with the impact horizon; widespread continental wildfire/soot and charcoal spikes
Genetic evidence: population bottleneck or extinction signatures in North American megafauna DNA, and any discontinuity in early Paleoindian genetic lineages around this date
Oral tradition: Indigenous North American narratives describing catastrophic sky-fire, darkness, or flood events, offered only as weak corroborative color, not proof

Model-prior literature: the existing Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (YDIH) papers proposing a cosmic airburst/impact as trigger for YD cooling and meltwater-driven AMOC weakening, and counter-papers disputing reproducibility of the impact markers
response.rationale: The hypothesis dates to exactly the conventional Younger Dryas onset (~12,900 cal BP), so I classified it under the 'younger-dryas' period row rather than leaving it unspecified. Quaternary geology and paleoceanography have good enough temporal resolution and preservation at this timescale that impact-proxy horizons (nanodiamonds, PGE anomalies, spherules, black mats) and AMOC-related sediment proxies are plausibly detectable (geological ~0.65, astronomical ~0.7 per the table) — and indeed this is precisely the terrain of the real, actively contested Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (model-prior, unverified as settled science). However, material/archaeological (0.35) and genetic (0.3) evidence from Paleoindian/megafaunal contexts is sparser and harder to unambiguously tie to a single-year causal event, and oral traditions (0.1) are weak and heavily filtered through millennia of transmission. The core difficulty is not preservation per se but causal specificity: distinguishing an airburst-triggered meltwater/AMOC mechanism from the many competing YD-onset explanations (Lake Agassiz drainage, orbital forcing, internal ocean variability) requires converging multi-proxy evidence that has in practice been reported by some teams but disputed/non-reproduced by others. Given the reasonably high geological/astronomical detectability offset by lower material/genetic detectability and genuine mechanistic ambiguity, I set an aggregate adjustment of 0.5 — evidence absence should be attributed partly to real detectability limits (especially for a 'no-crater' airburst) and partly to the hypothesis being one of several live scientific alternatives rather than confirmed fact.
